criteria.name: Deadline, extension, and re-opened-period timing language
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text explicitly orients itself to the clock of the comment period. Count only language about the FILING WINDOW, not compliance deadlines proposed inside the rule. Markers that count: naming the closing date; asserting timeliness ('submitted prior to the close of the comment period'); noting the hour or channel of filing; requesting an extension or additional time; identifying the document as supplemental, amended, corrected, or a re-submission; or invoking a re-opened or extended comment window. 10 = several such moves, prominent, often in the opening or closing paragraph. 5 = exactly one passing reference (e.g., a bare 'timely filed' or a date line tied to the deadline). 0 = nothing anywhere about dates, deadlines, timeliness, extensions, or an earlier filing by this same commenter; the text could have been written on any day of the period. Do not score references to what OTHER parties have filed (that is a different channel).
criteria.upstream_parent: Where the comment's filing timestamp falls relative to the opening and closing of the comment period, including whether it landed in an extended, re-opened, or post-deadline window.
criteria.rationale: Deadline-clock talk is a near-costless piece of procedural furniture: a thin comment can assert timeliness as easily as a thorough one, so the language itself carries no argument, evidence, or analysis. It should still predict, because it is emitted almost exclusively by filers writing against the closing date or filing a second time, and those filers are a non-random subset (organized, repeat, counsel-represented participants). Marked mixed because the underlying timing fact has a genuine route to quality in both directions: using the full period can mean deeper preparation, while a last-minute filing can mean a rushed one.

criteria.name: Awareness of the accumulated docket record
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the comment shows that a record already existed when it was written. Markers: naming, quoting, characterizing, or rebutting other commenters; responding to arguments 'raised by others in this docket'; citing testimony or statements from a public hearing, listening session, or roundtable already held; referring to a coalition, sign-on, or joint letter already submitted; citing the agency's own post-proposal actions (a supplemental notice, correction, data release, FAQ, or answers to earlier submissions); or citing outside developments that post-date the proposal ('in the nine months since the NPRM issued, ...'). 10 = the comment is substantially built around such material, with two or more distinct references to things that happened after the rule was published. 5 = one clear reference, otherwise self-contained. 0 = the comment engages only the proposed rule and the commenter's own material, with no sign that anything has occurred since publication. Do NOT count citations to prior rulemakings, statutes, case law, or academic literature that predate the proposal; those show expertise, not record awareness.
criteria.upstream_parent: Late ordinal position in the sequence of filings, and long elapsed time since the docket opened, so that a public record and post-proposal developments were available to read and cite.
criteria.rationale: This is a fingerprint of arrival order, not of reasoning quality: whether a commenter can quote another commenter is determined by who filed first, a fact entirely outside the comment's substance. It should predict because late filers in this process are disproportionately well-resourced institutional parties who monitor dockets. Marked mixed because engaging an existing record has a real merit route as well: rebutting opposing submissions and citing newer data genuinely can make a comment more useful to the agency.

criteria.name: De novo issue scaffolding versus incorporation by reference
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the comment builds its issue from the ground up as though nothing has been said yet, as opposed to attaching itself to something already said. 10 = fully de novo scaffolding: it restates or summarizes what the rule proposes, supplies its own framing and definitions of key terms, introduces the commenter and their stake at length, walks through background the agency already knows, and contains NO adoption, endorsement, echo, or incorporation of another party's submission. 5 = mostly standalone but with a brief nod to another filing, or standalone framing plus one 'we agree with' aside. 0 = a pure follower move, e.g. 'we join and incorporate by reference the comments of X', 'we adopt the analysis submitted by Y and write only to add one point', 'we endorse the coalition letter' — little or no standalone framing of the issue. Judge only the framing posture, not whether the analysis is correct or the writing is good.
criteria.upstream_parent: Early ordinal position in the filing sequence: little or nothing was in the record at drafting time, so there was nothing available to endorse, join, or incorporate.
criteria.rationale: Being first does not make an argument sounder, and the specific textual behavior scored here — explaining the agency's own proposal back to it, defining terms, long self-introduction — is closer to padding than to merit; conversely a one-line incorporation by reference can come from a highly expert party. The channel should still predict because filing order correlates with who the commenter is and how the agency processes the submission. Marked not mixed because the upstream fact ('nothing had yet been filed when I wrote') has no plausible direct route to the comment's substantive quality.

criteria.name: Mass-campaign petition register
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 on how strongly the text reads as one voice in an organized mass-participation drive rather than an individually composed submission to a decisionmaker. Markers: template or form-letter phrasing and boilerplate blocks with a small personalized insert; explicit crowd framing ('I join the thousands of Americans', 'add my name'); direct calls for the reader or others to act, sign, or share; head-count or vote-count framing ('count me among those opposed', 'the public has spoken'); slogan or campaign-title language; a single short paragraph of personal sentiment with no rule-specific detail, section citation, or factual claim; salutation addressed to a cause or to the public rather than to the agency. 10 = several of these, unmistakably a campaign artifact. 5 = individually written but clearly campaign-prompted (e.g., recites a campaign talking point and urges others to comment). 0 = no campaign markers at all: rule-specific, individualized, addressed to the agency as a decisionmaker. Do not reward or penalize the position taken.
criteria.upstream_parent: The comment sits in a large, high-salience, mass-participation docket where an advocacy campaign drove filings, so docket size is enormous relative to a specialist rulemaking.
criteria.rationale: Docket size is a property of the rule's political salience, not of any one comment's reasoning, so scoring the campaign register lets a rule-level attribute leak into a comment-level score. It should predict strongly because mass-participation dockets have a distinctive and highly detectable house style. Marked mixed because the campaign register co-occurs with genuinely thin content at the comment level: template letters usually do contain less rule-specific analysis, so a merit scorer would partly agree with this channel for the wrong reason.

criteria.name: Specialist insider shorthand assuming a small expert readership
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 for how strongly the text presumes a small, already-expert readership. Markers: program acronyms and technical shorthand used without expansion at first use; bare citation of sections, paragraphs, tables, or preamble page numbers with no explanation of what they are; direct address to a named office, division, docket manager, or staff contact; casual cross-reference to other dockets, prior rulemakings, meetings, or ex parte contacts as though the reader shares that history; jargon-dense sentences with no lay gloss; assumption that the reader already knows the commenter and their role. 10 = pervasive — a general reader could not follow the comment without a glossary. 5 = mixed register, some shorthand but key terms explained. 0 = everything is spelled out for a lay reader: acronyms expanded, the program and the proposal explained from scratch, no assumed shared history, no named-staff address. Score the ASSUMED AUDIENCE only, not whether the technical content is correct.
criteria.upstream_parent: The comment sits in a small specialist docket with few filers, where the writer expects a handful of agency technical staff — not a general public — to read it.
criteria.rationale: Assumed-audience register is set by the size and composition of the docket, a rule-level fact, and unexplained shorthand makes a comment less legible rather than more meritorious. It should predict because comments in tiny specialist dockets are read and handled very differently from comments in mass dockets. Marked not mixed because the upstream fact scored here is docket size, not the commenter's expertise: real analytic quality is produced by the commenter, and an expert can write a fully glossed comment while a non-expert can spray undefined acronyms, so the docket-size fact has no direct route to quality.
